newsitem.title: USA: NYS says to submit welfare plan early next week.
newsitem.headline: NYS says to submit welfare plan early next week.

text.p: New York State, which has been criticized for not moving swiftly enough on drafting a new welfare plan, on Wednesday said that it expected to submit a basic program to Washington by early next week.

The state stands to collect as much as $20 million a month for every month by which it beats the July 1 deadline, and as the clock started on October 1, any delay could have proved costly, as New York City Council officials have complained.

"We intend to file a plan with the federal government early next week in order to maximize bonus dollars for New York State," said Zenia Mucha, the spokeswoman for Gov. George Pataki. "So we'll be way over six months early on this."

The state had been concerned about whether the federal government would allow it to submit a plan before the legislature had approved the laws needed to put it into effect and before the end of a 45-day comment period.
New York had been looking to see how California would handle these issues, a state budget official had explained. California on Wednesday submitted its welfare plan.

Mucha denied that New York had advanced its timing. She explained that while the welfare task force will keep meeting, it holds its last session Thursday on the state's block grant and the overall requirements for the state and cities' roles, which clears the way for the state to submit a broad plan.
The governor has said he plans to call the legislature back into session in December to grapple with the difficult issues raised by the new federal welfare bill.
Pataki's attempts to impose workfare requirments and set time limits stalled in the Assembly this year, and his Adminisration has stressed the bipartisan nature of the welfare task force.
"We anticipate having to work with the legislature through December and January...but our goal always has been to submit a plan that would meet the broad requirements of the bill," Mucha said.

The governor's spokeswoman declined to release any details about how the state would structure its welfare program other than to say it would meet the federal guidlines, adding it was premature to release any financial estimates.

New York City Council members said they are concerned that the city, which accounts for about 66 percent of the state's welfare caseloads, would not receive a proportionate share of the state's $2.4 billion block grant in 1997.
Asked about this issue, Mucha replied the goal was to ensure each locality got what it needed.
